content:
If you were on GitHub Copilot for its flat $10 monthly fee, that deal ended June 1, 2026. Copilot now runs on credit billing, and one agentic session can drain your entire month's quota. For Indian developers, whether it's still worth paying depends entirely on how you actually use it.

Key Takeaways

  • Copilot's June 2026 billing switch killed flat-rate pricing; one agentic session can exhaust the $10/month plan's credits in a single afternoon.
  • Cursor launched a ₹649/month India plan on July 28, 2026, billed in rupees and payable by UPI.
  • Copilot Pro costs roughly ₹845 to ₹1,001/month in India after GST and forex; Cursor Start now undercuts that.
  • Autocomplete-only users are largely unaffected. Heavy agentic users face 10x to 50x higher effective costs.
  • Set a Copilot spending cap in GitHub billing settings now. There is no automatic ceiling on overages.

What Did GitHub Copilot's June 2026 Billing Change Actually Do?

GitHub moved all Copilot plans to usage-based billing on June 1. The $10/month Pro plan now buys 1,000 AI credits, each worth $0.01. A single agentic session that plans and implements a feature across multiple files typically burns $30 to $40 in credits. That's the whole month, gone in one working afternoon.

The reaction was loud. GitHub's community announcement collected nearly 900 downvotes and hundreds of comments. It's definately not just about money. For two years, developers could run Copilot as hard as they wanted for a fixed fee. That model subsidized heavy users at GitHub's expense, and it's over.

Agentic billing jumped between 10x and 50x for power users, based on before-and-after tracking shared in developer forums. The range is wide because the cost depends on which model handles each step. Routing every agent request through a frontier model like GPT-4o is far more expensive than running autocomplete through a smaller, faster one.

For light autocomplete use, the change is smaller than it sounds. Basic completions and single-file edits cost a fraction of what agentic work does. Developers who shift to autocomplete-only will recieve billing that's likely well within the base plan. The unpredictability is the real problem, not the average cost for light users.

Does Cursor's New India Plan Change the Decision?

On July 28, 2026, Cursor launched a ₹649/month plan called Cursor Start specifically for Indian developers. It's billed in rupees, payable by UPI, and includes Grok 4.5 and Composer alongside more agent requests than the free tier. Copilot Pro in India runs roughly ₹845 to ₹1,001 per month after forex markup and GST.

India is Cursor's third-largest market. The user base tripled in a year to over 3 million developers, and Indian developers run more agent requests per user than any other country. A rupee-priced plan with UPI support was a clear business priority for them.

Cursor Start has real limits. It doesn't include Bugbot, Auto Mode, or Automations. If you need background agents tied to CI pipelines, you're looking at the $20 Cursor Pro plan, not Start. But for a developer who wants solid Composer access and wants to pay in rupees without a forex headache, Start is a strong option at this price.

One catch: Cursor is its own editor, not a plugin for VS Code or JetBrains. Switching means adopting a new IDE. That's a bigger workflow disruption than a pricing page makes it look. Try the free tier for a week before paying for anything.

How Do Copilot and Cursor Compare for Indian Developers Right Now?

Cursor Start at ₹649/month (billed in INR, payable by UPI) now undercuts Copilot Pro's effective Indian cost of roughly ₹1,001/month including GST. Copilot still wins on IDE portability. For agentic work, Cursor's flat rate is more predictable. For multi-IDE teams or GitHub Enterprise users, Copilot's wider support still tips the balance.

When Does Copilot Still Make Sense?

Stay on Copilot if you mainly use it for autocomplete, test writing, and documentation, and you're using well under $10 in credits per month. That's roughly 200 credits or fewer. If your company pays for Copilot Business as part of a GitHub Enterprise deal, the personal cost calculation changes entirely anyway.

Copilot's clearest advantage is portability. It runs in VS Code, JetBrains, Neovim, Visual Studio, and the GitHub CLI. Cursor works only in the Cursor editor. If your team uses multiple setups, or your clients dictate the environment, that breadth matters in ways that don't show up in a simple cost table.

Copilot also handles inline refactoring of large existing codebases well, particularly on legacy projects where the full context is already loaded. For those use cases, almost no real loss in value occured after the billing switch. It got more expensive for agentic work; it didn't get worse at inline autocomplete.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I set a spending cap on Copilot to avoid surprise bills?

Yes, and you should do it immediately. Go to GitHub billing settings and set a monthly spending limit. Without a cap, overages charge at $0.01 per credit with no ceiling. Set it to zero overage so Copilot stops rather than bills you extra once your plan's credits run out.

Is Cursor Start worth trying if I've never used Cursor before?

At ₹649/month in INR with UPI support, the financial risk is low enough to try. Use the free tier for one week to see if the editor fits your workflow. Cursor Start is a reasonable step up for developers who want agentic features without committing to the $20 Pro plan or dealing with dollar billing.

Does Copilot Free still exist after the June billing change?

Yes. Copilot Free gives 2,000 completions and 50 chat messages per month, limited to Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4o. The June billing change primarily affected paid plan users. The free tier kept its terms and remains a solid option for occasional use or anyone evaluating the tool before committing to a paid plan.

How much time do AI coding tools actually save Indian developers?

Research puts time savings at 15 to 30 percent, concentrated on boilerplate, test coverage, and documentation. Gains are lower for architecture decisions and debugging novel systems. A 2025 Anthropic study found Indian developers compressed roughly 3.8 hours of work into 15-minute AI sessions, the highest rate globally.

For heavy agentic use, is Cursor Pro worth more than Cursor Start?

Yes. Cursor Pro at roughly ₹1,680 per month includes Bugbot, Auto Mode, and CI-linked agent workflows that Start doesn't offer. For a developer actively building and shipping rather than reviewing code, Pro's higher ceiling justifies the extra cost. Start suits developers who use agents occasionally, not several times a day.

The Short Version

GitHub Copilot's June 2026 billing change broke the math for anyone using agent mode regularly. A single session can now cost as much as the old monthly subscription. Cursor launched a ₹649 India plan billed in rupees with UPI support just days ago, undercutting Copilot's effective cost in India. If you're a heavy agentic user, the switch is worth seriously considering. If you mainly use autocomplete in VS Code or JetBrains, Copilot is still defensible. Either way, set a spending cap today.
